title: India Approves Rs 2,814-Crore Scheme for Lithium, Nickel Processing Plants
excerpt: The Cabinet cleared a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium and two nickel plants over FY 2026-27 to 2030-31, with winners chosen on the lowest support sought and paid in three milestone-linked tranches.
body:
• The Union Cabinet approved Rs 2,814 crore over five years, FY 2026-27 to 2030-31, as a 30% capital subsidy for four critical mineral processing plants.
  • Two lithium plants of at least 30 kt each are capped at Rs 500 crore per beneficiary; two nickel plants of at least 50 kt each are capped at Rs 900 crore.
  • Beneficiaries will be picked in two stages — technical qualification, then financial bidding on the lowest capex support sought — with payouts in three milestone-linked tranches.
  • The scheme targets lithium and nickel ores and intermediates converted into high-purity compounds, with cobalt recovered as a by-product of nickel processing.

India's Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved a Rs 2,814-crore incentive scheme to build domestic processing capacity for lithium and nickel, two minerals at the centre of battery and clean-technology supply chains. The Capex Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing will run for five years, from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, according to the official statement released after the Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The decision addresses a specific gap. India remains substantially dependent on imports for refined intermediates and high-purity materials because domestic beneficiation and processing infrastructure for lithium, nickel and cobalt is still at a nascent stage, the official statement said. Processing capacity is also geographically concentrated in a few locations globally, which the government said leaves supply chains exposed to geopolitical tensions, price volatility and export restrictions.

"Our National Critical Mineral Mission has been progressing in a very systematic manner... A scheme for the processing of critical minerals was approved by the Cabinet today."

— Ashwini Vaishnaw, Information and Broadcasting Minister

How the money is structured

The scheme pays a capital subsidy of 30% of eligible investment for setting up four plants. Two will process lithium, each with a minimum capacity of 30 kilotonnes, and two will process nickel, each with a minimum capacity of 50 kilotonnes. Support is capped at Rs 500 crore per lithium beneficiary and Rs 900 crore per nickel beneficiary, which means the four caps together account for Rs 2,800 crore of the Rs 2,814-crore outlay.

The plants will process lithium and nickel ores and intermediary products into high-purity compounds. Cobalt is expected to be recovered as a by-product of nickel production, the statement said. The government named electric mobility, battery energy storage systems (BESS), electronics, defence and speciality steel as the sectors the capacity is intended to support.

Selection and payment terms

Beneficiaries will not be chosen on a first-come basis. Selection will run in two stages: applications will first be assessed for technical qualification, and only technically qualified applicants will move to financial bidding. For each mineral, two beneficiaries will be selected on the least-cost criterion — the lowest capex support sought by bidders under the scheme. Incentives will be disbursed in three tranches linked to the achievement of specified milestones, according to the statement.

Those terms matter for investors assessing the announcement. The subsidy reduces upfront capital cost but does not remove the other constraints the government itself listed: high capital requirements, limited availability of suitable technologies and constrained access to raw materials for commercial-scale projects. Because winners are picked on the least support sought, the effective subsidy for some projects could also come in below the headline 30%.

What the scheme does not yet answer

The Cabinet approval sets the outlay, plant count, capacities and caps, but the reports of the decision do not state when applications will open, where the plants will be located, or which companies will bid. The scheme is an approval to spend over five years, not commissioned capacity. Its effect on import dependence will depend on execution — whether qualified bidders come forward at the caps offered, whether feedstock can be secured, and whether the milestone schedule holds through 2030-31.

For global supply chains, the significance is directional. Processing, rather than mining alone, is where value and leverage concentrate in battery materials, and India has historically exported or imported around this step rather than performing it at scale. A domestic processing base for lithium and nickel compounds would give Indian cell, vehicle and electronics manufacturers a local source of high-purity inputs, and give overseas buyers an additional processing location outside the current concentrated geography. The Cabinet paired the decision with a separate push on energy storage, but the minerals scheme stands on its own numbers: Rs 2,814 crore, four plants, and a five-year window to turn approval into operating capacity.
